issues: The notes say 'The authors compare it with 2007 U.S. online retail sales of about $260 billion.' That misreads the paper. The $260 billion sentence does not compare against the $781 billion total. It reads 'In 2007, United States online sales were approximately $260 billion—more than the cost to businesses if their employees were to read privacy policies on corporate time'. That clause itself conflicts with the paper's own Table 8, which puts the work-time cost at $617B. The paper also says 'online sales', not 'retail sales'. The comparison the authors actually draw for the $781 billion is with U.S. online advertising: 'The value of all online advertising in the United States was about $21 billion in 2007', and Internet users 'should give up an estimated $781 billion of their time to protect themselves from an industry worth substantially less.'

Checked and correct: the quote was FOUND in the draft and in the published version. $781B is the point estimate (range $559.7B-$1.1T), split into work $617B and home $164B. $3,534 per user = work $2,791 + home $743. Time is valued at 1/4 of wages at home and 2x wages at work, from a BLS average hourly wage of $17.93 for March 2008.

fieldFixes.notes: Point estimate (range $559.7 billion to $1.1 trillion; work time $617 billion, home time $164 billion). Values leisure time at 25% of the average hourly wage ($17.93, BLS, March 2008) and time at work at twice the wage; about $3,534 per internet user per year. The authors set it against the roughly $21 billion value of all U.S. online advertising in 2007, the industry whose data collection the policies disclose.

issues: The notes give the range as '8 minutes for a first-quartile policy of 2,071 words', which leaves out the upper end. Table 1 runs from 8 minutes (2,071 words, 'first quartile') to 12 minutes (3,112 words, 'third quartile'). The text says 'it takes about eight to twelve minutes'. The paper defines these 'quartiles' in its own way, as the average of all data points below or above the median (footnote 37).

The geography '75 most popular U.S. websites (2008)' is inaccurate. The paper took the 75 most popular sites from 'a list of 30,000 most frequently clicked-on websites from AOL search data in October, 2005'. The paper does not say the sites are U.S. sites, and the popularity ranking dates from October 2005, not 2008.

Checked and correct: the quote was FOUND in the draft and in the published version. 2,514-word median at 250 wpm = 10 minutes. The skimming study had 212 participants, from whom 44 outliers were removed. The paper is inconsistent on the point estimate: it says 'with the mean value as a point estimate', but Table 1 uses the median. The label's 'average' follows the abstract's wording and is acceptable.

fieldFixes.geography: 75 most popular websites, from a list of the 30,000 most frequently clicked-on sites in AOL search data (October 2005); policies measured for the 2008 paper
fieldFixes.notes: Median policy length 2,514 words at 250 words per minute. Range 8-12 minutes: 2,071 words for a 'first-quartile' policy and 3,112 words for a 'third-quartile' one (the paper defines these as the averages below and above the median). The authors say the times may be slightly low because of jargon and slower reading on screen. They also measured skimming time in an online study of 212 participants (44 outliers removed).
